bibliographic.authors: Ashish Sharma, Prashant Kumar (Global Centre for Clean Air Research (GCARE), Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, University of Surrey, Guildford, UK; corresponding author P. Kumar)
bibliographic.year: 2018 (received 13 May 2018; revised 25 July 2018; accepted 26 July 2018; available online 10 August 2018)
bibliographic.title: A review of factors surrounding the air pollution exposure to in-pram babies and mitigation strategies
bibliographic.volumeIssuePages: Volume 120, pp. 262-278 (PDF page = journal page minus 261)
bibliographic.funding: Acknowledgement p.275: MAPE Project (Mitigation of Air Pollution Exposure to young children); PhD studentship funding from University of Surrey; EPSRC (UK); industrial collaborators Brizi Ltd., United Kingdom. The review names a clean-air pram device ('BRIZI baby', p.273). The authors state they do not endorse commercial products named. No conflict-of-interest or competing-interests statement appears in the PDF text.
bibliographic.openAccess: Not stated in the PDF (copyright line: Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved)

studyDesign: Narrative review of scientific and grey literature (journal and conference papers, technical reports, policy statements, catalogues, brochures; p.263). No search protocol, databases, date range or inclusion criteria are printed. Scope: personal exposure of in-pram babies (under 1 year) and toddlers (1-3 years) to traffic-related PM10, PM2.5, ultrafine particles, black carbon and NOx outdoors; indoor exposure excluded (p.264). Table 1 summarises 10 exposure studies on children/babies: Kumar 2017 (Guildford, UK), Kenagy 2016 (Edinburgh), Rivas 2016 (Barcelona), Galea 2014 (Edinburgh), Garcia-Algar 2015 (Barcelona), Rivas 2014 (Barcelona), Buonanno 2013 (Casino, Italy), Burtscher & Schuepp 2012 (Zurich), Buzzard 2009 (Morgantown, West Virginia, USA), Chaix 2006 (Malmo, Sweden). Only four are compared with adults in Table 3 (Kumar 2017; Kenagy 2016; Garcia-Algar 2015; Buzzard 2009); Galea 2014 is discussed in text as the contrary result. The authors' own original content is the pram classification from manufacturer catalogues (Table 2) and syntheses of flow/dispersion, particle chemistry, mitigation technology and community/policy measures. No new measurements, no meta-analysis, no pooled estimate; every concentration comparison is cited from the original studies. Supplementary Tables S1-S7 and Sections S1-S5 were not in the PDF. Pollutants covered: PM, UFP, BC, NO2/NOx; no benzene, CO or hydrocarbon concentrations at the kerb are reported (Buzzard's CO/CO2/NOx are listed as measured in Table 1 but no results are given). Vehicle type is never specified as gasoline or scooter; the emission discussion centres on diesel and heavy-duty vehicles. The words scooter, motorcycle, moped, electric vehicle and Taiwan do not appear in the text (searched).

findings.claim: The review states in-pram babies' breathing height is between 0.55 and 0.85 m above ground. The main text does not tabulate breathing height by pram type; the range coincides with the sensor heights of the Table 3 studies (0.55 m, 0.8 m, 0.85 m).
findings.value: Breathing height 0.55 m to 0.85 m (babies/children); adult heights printed in Table 3 / Table 1: 1.65 m (Buzzard), 1.70 m (Garcia-Algar), 2.0 m (Kenagy)
findings.quote: in-pram babies or children breathing height between 0.55 m and 0.85 m above the ground level
findings.locator: Abstract; Section 3 last paragraph (p.266); Section 8 bullet 2 (p.274)
findings.caveats: The abstract and Section 8 say the pram classification 'pointed out' / 'assessed' the breathing height, but Table 2 gives only pram handle/top heights (59-124 cm), not seated-baby breathing heights; the p.266 sentence attaches 0.55-0.85 m to the Table 3 studies. So the source of the range is stated inconsistently. No toddler-specific height. Fig. 2a bars suggest ~0.7 m baby and ~1.4 m adult for Kumar et al. 2017 (read from bar chart, not printed).
findings.useOnSite: Studies the review summarises put a baby's breathing height at roughly 0.55 to 0.85 m.
findings.checkerNote: Page for Section 8 bullet 2 is 274, not 275. Reader's statement that the range is 'not from a separate measurement' is a fair inference but the authors themselves say it came from the pram classification; both statements are in the paper and they do not agree. Adult range '1.65-2.0 m' holds only for the three studies that print an adult height; Kumar 2017 adult height is not printed (about 1.4 m on Fig. 2a).

findings.claim: The review says the first metre above the road is where most road-vehicle tailpipes sit, the same zone as pram heights, and that the air in the first (few) metres above the road is usually most polluted.
findings.value: Tailpipe height: 'first 1 m above the road level'; pram handle height 59-124 cm (Table 2)
findings.quote: the concentration within the first 1 m above the road level, the same height where tailpipe of most road vehicles resides, lies within the zone of pram heights
findings.caveats: No tailpipe height in metres for any vehicle class; no scooter mentioned; not referenced to a measurement. The abstract says 'first few meters', Section 2 says 'first meter'. The review itself later says the height gradient 'does not really exist' in the first two metres (p.268). Buzzard et al. 2009 is cited for breathing height relative to the exhaust pipe.
findings.useOnSite: The authors state that most vehicle tailpipes sit within the first metre above the road, the same band as a baby in a pram.
findings.checkerNote: Quote and page verified. Added the first-metre / first-few-metres wording difference.

findings.claim: From manufacturer catalogues the authors classify prams: top height 59-124 cm, width 56-82 cm, weight 3.9-19.5 kg, for ages 0-5 years.
findings.value: Height 59-124 cm; width 56-82 cm; weight 3.9-19.5 kg; ages 0-5 y
findings.quote: height of the pram top varies from 59 cm to 124 cm; and (4) width of typical pram varies from 56 cm to 82 cm
findings.caveats: Table 2 column is headed 'handle height'; text calls it 'height of the pram top'. These are not the baby's breathing height. Data from retail websites. Abstract says 'top handle heights up to ~1.25 m'.
findings.useOnSite: Prams on sale are 56-82 cm wide and up to about 1.2 m at the handle, so the baby sits well below adult head height.
findings.checkerNote: Verified against Table 2: ranges match (e.g. ATP 92.5-123.5 cm, travel systems 56-60 cm wide, 3.9 kg).

findings.claim: At Guildford, in-pram babies had 10% higher PM2.5 than adults in the afternoon but 5% significantly lower in the morning (Kumar, Rivas & Sachdeva 2017).
findings.value: Afternoon PM2.5: babies 9-20 ug/m3 vs adults 8-17 ug/m3, '10% higher for babies than adults'. Morning: babies 10-36 vs adults 10-46 ug/m3, '5% significantly lower than adults'
findings.quote: Table 3: 'Morning (PM2.5) 10-36 | 10-46 | 5% significantly lower than adults'; 'Afternoon (PM2.5) 9-20 | 8-17 | 10% higher for babies than adults'
findings.caveats: Table 3 column headed 'Mean concentration' but Kumar rows print ranges only; Fig. 2a plots about 20 vs 17 ug/m3 (the upper ends of the afternoon ranges). 'Significantly' printed only for the morning (lower) result; no p-value or CI. Baby and adult heights not printed in Table 3. Table 1: Guildford (U.K.), 87 km (1159 +/- 74 min); instruments GRIMM EDM 107, P-Trak, Dylos DC1700, SEM. Ref: Kumar, P., Rivas, I., Sachdeva, L., 2017. Environ. Pollut. 224, 407-420. The morning result goes against the site's argument.
findings.useOnSite: In one UK study, baby-height PM2.5 was about 10% higher than adult height in the afternoon but about 5% lower in the morning.
findings.checkerNote: Numbers, row labels and page verified on PDF page 6 and Fig. 2a. Added the range-versus-mean point.

findings.claim: At a kerbside on an urban main road in Edinburgh, NO2 at child breathing height (0.8 m) was 5-15% higher than at adult height (2.0 m).
findings.value: NO2 57 vs 52 ug/m3 (Table 3); '5-15% higher'
findings.quote: The NO2 concentrations at the height of children breathing zone (0.8 m) higher (5-15%) in comparison with the NO2 concentrations at the adult breathing zone (2.0 m).
findings.caveats: Passive diffusion tubes (time-averaged, stationary, not a walking measurement). 57/52 is about 10%. Ref: Kenagy, H.S., Lin, C., Wu, H., Heal, M.R., 2016. Air Qual. Atmos. Health 9, 589-595 (title: 'Greater nitrogen dioxide concentrations at child versus adult breathing heights close to urban main road kerbside'). No significance test reported in the review. NO2 is not specific to gasoline vehicles.
findings.useOnSite: A kerbside tube study in Edinburgh found NO2 5-15% higher at child height than at adult height.
findings.checkerNote: Verified in Table 1 (PDTs, Edinburgh) and Table 3.

findings.claim: Walking on Barcelona streets, infants in strollers (0.55 m) breathed about 10% more ultrafine particles than adults (1.70 m).
findings.quote: 10% higher at the height of in pram babies (0.55 m) than the height of adults (1.70 m)
findings.locator: Table 1 row 5; Table 3 row 4 and footnote a; Section 3 (p.266)
findings.caveats: Size range is stated two ways: Table 1 gives UFP 20-1000 nm; Table 3 footnote gives 0.02-0.1 um (20-100 nm). 3 walking routes, 20 km (1200 min), P-TRAK 8525. Standard deviations overlap heavily; no significance test given. 4.82/4.31 is about 12% by printed means. The p.266 text says 'exposure to UFPs and PM2.5 ... up to 10% higher' for this study, but Table 1 lists only UFP for it. Ref: Garcia-Algar, O. et al., 2015. Environ. Monit. Assess. 187, 4196.
findings.useOnSite: A Barcelona walking study measured about 10% more ultrafine particles at stroller height than at adult height.
findings.checkerNote: Added the size-range discrepancy between Table 1 and Table 3 and the PM2.5 mention on p.266 that Table 1 does not support. Numbers and heights confirmed.

findings.claim: In Morgantown, West Virginia, near a roadway, PM2.5 at stroller-baby height (0.85 m) was 59% higher than at adult height (1.65 m); this is the largest difference in the review and the source of the headline 'up to ~60%'.
findings.value: PM2.5 199 vs 125 ug/m3; '59% higher'
findings.quote: 59% higher at the height of baby in a stroller (0.85 m) than the height of adult (1.65 m)
findings.locator: Table 3 last row; Table 1 row 9; Fig. 2b
findings.caveats: Table 1: measurements at different heights near a roadway; pollutants PM (mass and particle number counts, 1-1000 nm), CO, CO2, NOx; instruments fast-response particle spectrometer (Cambustion DS500), Horiba AIA-200, EcoPhysics CLD-822. Key finding: people breathing at the height of a passing vehicle's tailpipe 'may be exposed to higher' PM than standing adults. The reference title is 'Investigation into pedestrian exposure to near-vehicle exhaust emissions'. The review does not say whether prams, mannequins or fixed inlets were used, nor averaging time, vehicle mix or statistics. Table 3 labels it PM2.5, Table 1 lists PM1/UFP. No CO or NOx results are given. Ref: Buzzard, N.A., Clark, N.N., Guffey, S.E., 2009. Environ. Health 8, 13. Vehicle fuel type not stated.
findings.useOnSite: One US roadside study cited by the review found PM2.5 59% higher at 0.85 m than at 1.65 m near a roadway.
findings.checkerNote: Reader wrote 'near passing vehicles'; the table says 'near a roadway' (the key-finding sentence refers to a passing vehicle's tailpipe height). Added the measured-pollutant list and the reference title (pedestrian exposure). Numbers confirmed.

findings.claim: In Edinburgh (Galea et al. 2014), children in buggies were not exposed to higher PM2.5 than the adults pushing them; adults were 17-51% higher on some days and children 16% higher on one of six days.
findings.value: Adults 17-51% higher PM2.5 on some days; children 16% higher on 1 of 6 measurement days; no difference on other days
findings.quote: Galea et al. (2014) reported 17-51% higher PM2.5 exposure of adults than children in buggies on some days while they did not notice such differences on the other days. In fact, children exposure to PM2.5 was found to be 16% higher than that of adult on one of their six days measurements
findings.caveats: 3 routes, SidePak AM510 with PM2.5 impactor; (6480) min. Buggy height not stated in the review. Authors 'did not explain the reason for this changing trend'. The review's own explanation is that concentration usually decreases with height, which would make the adult-higher result unexpected. Ref: Galea et al. 2014. J. Environ. Health Res. 14, 28-42 ('Are children in buggies exposed to higher PM2.5 concentrations than adults'). Excluded from Table 3.
findings.useOnSite: Not every study finds a difference: an Edinburgh study found adults breathed equal or higher PM2.5 than children in buggies on most days.
findings.checkerNote: Quote verified verbatim on PDF page 5. The useOnSite wording 'on most days' is slightly beyond the paper (it says 'some days' for adults higher and 'on the other days' no difference); read 'on some days adults higher, otherwise no difference'.

findings.claim: The review summarises that in-pram babies can be exposed to up to ~60% (~59%) higher average concentrations than adults depending on pollutant and other factors; the Table 3 range is 5-59% higher with one result 5% lower.
findings.value: 'up to ~60%' (abstract, Section 8); 'up to ~59%' (Section 3); Table 3: 59%, 5-15%, 10%, 10% higher; 5% lower (Kumar morning)
findings.quote: up to ~59% higher exposure than adults, depending on factors such as: (i) concentration decay with height, (ii) proximity with the roadways, (iii) location of the vehicle tailpipe close to the passenger side, and (iv) duration of exposure measurement
findings.caveats: The maximum rests on one study (Buzzard 2009). 'Irrespective of pollutants, the majority of studies show increased exposure concentrations of in-pram babies than adults' (p.265-266) is a statement about four Table 3 studies with different pollutants, heights and averaging times, no CIs. Section 8 gives the authors' causal explanation (concentrations in the first 1 m where tailpipes lie), which no Table 3 study tests.
findings.useOnSite: The authors summarise baby-height exposure as up to about 59% higher than adults, depending on distance from the road, tailpipe position and averaging time; the other quantified studies show about 5-15%, and one showed babies lower in the morning.
findings.checkerNote: Page for Section 8 is 274 not 275. Reader's 'most studies finding 5-12%' replaced by the printed 5-15% (NO2), 10% (UFP), 10% (afternoon PM2.5). Added that the causal explanation is the authors' and is untested.

findings.claim: Roadside pollutant concentrations usually decrease with height, higher in the lower part owing to proximity to emission sources, but in the first two metres traffic turbulence means the decreasing profile 'does not really exist'.
findings.value: Vertical profile of particle number measured at 0.20 m, 1.0 m and 2.60 m (Kumar et al. 2008b), exponential fit to daily averages
findings.quote: Although the first two meters close to the road are highly turbulent due to traffic-produced turbulence and the same decreasing profile of concentrations does not really exist
findings.caveats: Complicates a simple 'lower = more polluted' claim: the review says the profile is not reliable within the first 2 m. Exponential height decay for CO (Zoumakis 1995, Athens street canyon) is cited; fitted parameters are in supplementary S1, not seen.
findings.useOnSite: Concentrations generally fall with height above a road, though within the first two metres traffic turbulence mixes the air so the gradient is not always clear.
findings.checkerNote: Verified verbatim.

findings.claim: Pollutants decay horizontally from the kerb, so prams on the kerbside experience the highest concentrations.
findings.value: n/a (qualitative; Kenagy et al. 2016 cited)
findings.quote: the prams being on kerbside environments mean that the prams experience the highest concentrations before its decay to further distances
findings.caveats: No distances or percentages given.
findings.useOnSite: The review notes concentrations fall with distance from the kerb, so a pram beside the road gets the highest levels.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Roadside prams are directly affected by the wake of on-road vehicles; dilution in the near wake of a moving vehicle is very fast; in the far wake mixing is mainly by atmospheric turbulence.
findings.value: Near wake to ~10-15h, far wake >15h (h = vehicle height, Fig. 3b labels)
findings.quote: the dilution stage in the near-wake of a moving vehicle is very fast and it dominates competing effects associated with other transformation processes
findings.caveats: Concerns a moving car (Carpentieri et al. 2011; Kumar et al. 2009b), not an idling queue. Idling is not discussed. The text says the far wake 'extends to few times the height of the vehicle'; the 10-15h and >15h numbers are Fig. 3 labels.
findings.useOnSite: The review explains that emissions from moving vehicles dilute quickly in the wake, which is why the zone close to the tailpipe matters.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Wind speed and direction, street geometry and traffic volume affect how much exhaust reaches the pram; crosswind steers pollutants to the kerb.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: factors such as meteorological conditions (e.g., wind speed and direction), the built-up features along the roadside and traffic volume crucially affect the dilution, dispersion and exposure of pollutants to in-pram babies
findings.caveats: Qualitative, supported by Buzzard et al. 2009 and others; no numbers.
findings.useOnSite: Wind, street layout and traffic volume all change how much exhaust reaches a pram.
findings.checkerNote: Verified (quote on p.270).

findings.claim: At Guildford, traffic intersections were hotspots of enhanced exposure for coarse particles (PM2.5-10) and particle number concentration (PNC); a bus stand was also assessed.
findings.value: Qualitative; Table 1 key finding
findings.quote: Traffic intersections found to be hotspots of enhanced exposure for PM2.5-10 and PNC concentration.
findings.caveats: No numbers for the intersection excess. Study details say it assessed 'specific contribution of traffic intersections, and bus stand'; no bus-stand result is given. Not stated for PM2.5. The review hypothesises (p.265) that pram covers at 'traffic intersections and bus stands' could act as barriers, citing BBC 2017 and Kumar 2017; this is untested. No mention of idling, red-light queues or waiting at crossings.
findings.useOnSite: A UK stroller study identified traffic intersections as hotspots for particle number and coarse particles.
findings.checkerNote: Verified in Table 1.

findings.claim: At Guildford, morning drop-in runs had 47% higher PM2.5, 31% higher PM1 and 31% higher PNC than afternoon runs, but coarse particles were 70% higher in the afternoons.
findings.value: PM2.5 +47%, PM1 +31%, PNC +31% (morning vs afternoon); PM2.5-10 +70% (afternoon vs morning)
findings.quote: PM2.5, PM1 and PNC concentrations were 47, 31 and 31% higher during the morning runs than those during the afternoon hours due to higher traffic emissions during the morning Peak hours.
findings.caveats: These are absolute morning-versus-afternoon contrasts, whereas Table 3 gives baby-versus-adult contrasts for the same study; both can be true together. The Introduction (p.263) sentence says in-pram babies are exposed to higher PM2.5 'during the afternoon pick-up hours ... compared with morning drop-off hours': read literally it contradicts Table 1; read as a baby-versus-adult statement it matches Table 3. Ambiguous; do not use that sentence. Section 5 (p.269) says traffic volume was similar in both periods and attributes afternoon coarse particles to suppressed resuspension in the morning (dew, wet road), while Table 1 attributes higher morning fine particles to 'higher traffic emissions during the morning Peak hours'; the review does not reconcile these.
findings.useOnSite: The Guildford study found fine-particle and particle-number exposure highest in the morning rush, coarse particles higher in the afternoon.
findings.checkerNote: Reader called the Introduction sentence an outright contradiction. It is ambiguous: it can be read as baby-versus-adult (consistent with Table 3). Also added the p.269 'similar traffic volume' versus Table 1 'higher traffic emissions' tension. Numbers confirmed.

findings.claim: Outdoor PM2.5 at Barcelona schools was almost double the usual background level, and outdoor UFP and NO2 were higher than indoors (Rivas et al. 2014).
findings.value: 'almost double the usual background levels reported for Barcelona' (PM2.5)
findings.quote: Outdoor PM2.5 levels at schools almost double the usual background levels reported for Barcelona.
findings.caveats: Stationary school measurements, not at pram height; no numbers given in the review (PM2.5 high-volume sampler, 71,040 min). The pollutant is PM2.5, not 'PM'. Ref: Rivas et al. 2014. Environ. Int. 69, 200-212 ('Child exposure to indoor and outdoor air pollutants in schools in Barcelona'). School drop-off hotspots for prams are covered only by Kumar 2017.
findings.useOnSite: A Barcelona study found outdoor PM2.5 at schools about double the usual city background.
findings.checkerNote: Reader's quote said 'PM'; the table says PM2.5 (subscript). Fixed claim, quote and wording.

findings.claim: Near a busy road UFP number concentration 'can reach' 50,000 per cm3 and, the authors of the cited study state, a child will hence inhale about 2.5 x 10^8 particles per minute (Burtscher & Schuepp 2012).
findings.value: 50,000 particles/cm3 (peak, 'can reach'); 2.5 x 10^8 particles/min inhaled
findings.quote: Near a busy road, the number concentration of UFP can reach 50,000/cm3 and a child will hence inhale about 2.5 x 10^8 particles per minute.
findings.caveats: A calculation from a peak concentration, not a measured inhaled dose and not an average; the breathing rate implied (about 5 L/min) is not printed in the review. Zurich, child on a bicycle trailer (UFP 10-700 nm, DiSCmini), not a pram. Study notes UFP exposure is mostly underestimated by mass-based methods.
findings.useOnSite: Near a busy road, a child can breathe in the order of 250 million ultrafine particles per minute at peak concentrations (calculated, Zurich study).
findings.checkerNote: Chain link changed (it is a dose/exposure statement, not a compound-toxicity one). Added that it is a calculation from a peak ('can reach') value and the breathing rate is not stated. Numbers confirmed.

findings.claim: Children inhale a higher dose of airborne particles relative to lung size and body weight; respiratory rate per body weight is generally two-fold higher than for adults.
findings.value: Respiratory rate per body weight ~2-fold higher than adults
findings.quote: the respiratory rate of child per body weight is generally two-fold higher than that for adults (Ginsberg et al., 2005)
findings.caveats: Ref: Ginsberg, G.L., Perkovich Foos, B., Firestone, M.P., 2005. J. Toxic. Environ. Health A 68, 573-615 (review of inhalation dosimetry methods). No absolute breathing rates, age bands or lung-size data are printed. The sentence is framed around UFP vulnerability in children generally, not babies in prams specifically.
findings.useOnSite: Per kilogram of body weight, children breathe roughly twice as fast as adults (Ginsberg et al. 2005, as cited).
findings.checkerNote: Verified verbatim.

findings.claim: Children have immature tissues, lungs, immune system and brain that develop quickly, and permeable cell membranes lining the respiratory tract.
findings.value: n/a (qualitative)
findings.quote: (ii) they have immature tissues, lungs, immune system, and brain which continue developing quickly; and (iii) they have permeable cell membrane lining inside their respiratory tract
findings.caveats: Cited to Bates 1995; Buonanno et al. 2013; Burtscher & Schuepp 2012; Mendell & Heath 2005; WHO 2005. No numbers.
findings.useOnSite: The review lists immature lungs, immune system and brain, and more permeable airway membranes as reasons children are more vulnerable.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: A computational fluid dynamics model found infants at greater risk from airborne PM, with deposition in tracheobronchial airways decreasing with age.
findings.value: n/a (no numbers in review)
findings.quote: infants are potentially at a greater health risk from exposure to airborne particulate matter and the particle deposition decreases with increasing age
findings.caveats: Modelled, not measured. Ref: Deng, Q., Ou, C., Chen, J., Xiang, Y., 2018. Sci. Total Environ. 612, 339-346 ('Particle deposition in tracheobronchial airways of an infant, child and adult').
findings.useOnSite: A 2018 airway-modelling study found particle deposition is greater in infants and declines with age.
findings.checkerNote: Verified. 'Computation fluid dynamics modelling' is the review's wording.

findings.claim: UFPs have greater surface area, higher pulmonary deposition efficiency, can enter the circulation and accumulate in lymph nodes and brain tissue; toxicity per unit mass increases as particle size falls.
findings.value: n/a (qualitative)
findings.quote: PM2.5 is usually more toxic than PM10 while UFPs shows the highest toxicity per unit mass which increases with decreased size range
findings.locator: Section 1 paragraphs 1-2 (Harrison & Yin 2000; Heal et al. 2012)
findings.caveats: Framing from cited reviews. The review also says ambient standards for BC and UFPs are missing (Kumar et al. 2018a).
findings.useOnSite: The review notes toxicity per unit mass rises as particles get smaller, with ultrafine particles the highest.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: A study of hospital admissions for asthma in children (Iskandar et al.) found a significant positive association with traffic-related pollutants; the review gives, per IQR increase in the 5-day mean before admission: NOx 1.11 (95% CI 1.05-1.17), NO2 1.10 (1.04-1.16), PM2.5 1.09 (1.04-1.13), PM10 1.07 (1.03-1.12); UFP association 'weak positive and non-significant'.
findings.value: Risk estimates 1.07-1.11 per IQR of 5-day mean; CIs exclude 1 for NOx, NO2, PM2.5, PM10; UFP non-significant (no number)
findings.caveats: The review does not name the city or country, the metric (rate ratio / relative risk) or the IQR values; the review calls these 'the following highest risk estimate'. Effect is per interquartile-range increase, not per ug/m3. Children's asthma admissions, not pram babies. The reference title is 'Coarse and fine particles but not ultrafine particles in urban air trigger hospital admission for asthma in children' (Iskandar, Andersen, Bonnelykke, Ellermann, Andersen, Bisgaard; Thorax 2012, 67, 252-257; cited in text as 2011). The UFP result weakens a UFP-specific argument.
findings.significance: Significant for NOx, NO2, PM2.5, PM10 (CIs exclude 1); UFP non-significant; per IQR of 5-day mean
findings.useOnSite: A study cited by the review found children's asthma admissions associated with recent NOx, NO2, PM2.5 and PM10 (risk estimates 1.07-1.11 per interquartile increase in the 5-day mean); no significant association with ultrafine particles.
findings.checkerNote: Reader's claim named Copenhagen; the paper does not name the city, so it is removed. Corrected the reference (Thorax 2012, 67, 252-257). Numbers confirmed. 'Rose by 7-11%' is an interpretation of a ratio whose type the review does not state.

findings.claim: A meta-analysis (Khreis et al. 2017), as cited: NO2 1.05 (95% CI 1.02-1.07) per 4 ug/m3; PM2.5 1.03 (1.01-1.05) per 1 ug/m3; PM10 1.05 (1.02-1.08) per 2 ug/m3; NOx 1.48 (0.89-2.45) per 30 ug/m3 (CI includes 1).
findings.caveats: The review calls all four 'statistically significant' but the NOx interval includes 1. Outcome is risk of asthma development; metric (RR/OR) not stated. Ref: Khreis et al. 2017. Environ. Int. 100, 1-31 (systematic review and meta-analysis).
findings.significance: Significant for NO2, PM2.5, PM10; NOx CI 0.89-2.45 not significant
findings.useOnSite: A meta-analysis cited by the review found childhood asthma risk about 5% higher per 4 ug/m3 NO2 and about 3% higher per 1 ug/m3 PM2.5.
findings.checkerNote: Verified verbatim; NOx non-significance flag is correct.

findings.claim: Studies of school-age children (not babies) found higher traffic-pollution exposure associated with slower cognitive growth, altered brain connectivity and weaker cognition.
findings.value: Sunyer et al. 2015: children aged 7-10 y, Barcelona, 'from 2715 schools' as printed; Suglia et al. 2007: 202 children, mean age ~9.7 +/- 1.7 y, Boston, BC annual mean 0.56 +/- 0.13 ug/m3; Pujol et al. 2016: lower functional integration and segregation, slower brain maturation
findings.quote: children with higher levels of exposure had a smaller growth in cognitive development over time (Sunyer et al., 2015)
findings.caveats: No effect sizes or CIs. School children, observational. 'In-pram babies are expected to be exposed too, damaging their frontal lobe as well as cognition and brain development' (p.268) is an extrapolation. The '2715 schools' count is quoted as printed and should be checked against the original paper before use. Calderon-Garcidueñas 2013 concerns Mexico City residents (primarily children), olfactory function and metals such as Mn.
findings.useOnSite: Studies of school-age children in Barcelona and Boston link traffic pollution to slower cognitive development; the review extrapolates this concern to babies but did not measure it.
findings.checkerNote: Verified figures against p.263. Added the flag to check the '2715 schools' figure at source.

findings.claim: Roadside particles are dominated by metals, but the review's own sources attribute most trace-element enrichment to vehicle wear and resuspension rather than exhaust.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: enrichment of most trace elements in roadside aerosol is derived from vehicle wear products as opposed to exhaust emissions
findings.caveats: Cu, Zn, Mo, Ba, Pb correlated with NOx and particle count (Harrison 2003); tyre wear a major source of Zn. Kumar et al. 2017 SEM/EDS found Cl, Na and Fe dominant. The review nonetheless concludes the 'dominance of toxic metals' and neurotoxic damage. Metals shown are largely brake, tyre and road dust, which electric vehicles also produce.
findings.useOnSite: The review notes that most metals in roadside dust come from tyre, brake and road wear, not the tailpipe.
findings.checkerNote: Verified on PDF page 6.

findings.claim: Increases in roadside PM2.5 are 'usually dominated by exhaust emissions', whereas coarse particles come from resuspension, brake and tyre wear.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: The increase in roadside concentrations of fine particles (PM2.5) is usually dominated by exhaust emissions (Amato et al., 2009; Kumar and Goel, 2016; Kumar et al., 2018b) as opposed to coarse particles (PM2.5-10) coming from sources such as resuspension of road dust, brake and tyre wear (Kumar et al., 2017)
findings.caveats: Not specific to gasoline or two-wheelers.
findings.useOnSite: The review says roadside fine particles are mainly from exhaust, coarse particles from road dust, brakes and tyres.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: The review's source-emission discussion concerns diesel and heavy-duty vehicles; it does not discuss gasoline scooters.
findings.value: n/a
findings.quote: Published literature has established that diesel vehicles are a primary source of emissions of PM, NOx and pollutants such as sulfur dioxide and hydrocarbons.
findings.caveats: Not usable for gasoline scooter claims. The text says emission control technologies can reduce 'CO and hydrocarbons by > 95% and NOx emissions for > 80%' (p.270) without saying for which vehicles; Table 4 (PM and NOx after-treatment: DOC, DPF, EGR, SCR, LNC) is diesel-oriented and gives no CO or hydrocarbon figures.
findings.useOnSite: Do not cite this review for gasoline scooter emissions: its source discussion is about diesel and heavy-duty vehicles.
findings.checkerNote: Verified. Note the CO/HC >95% figure is in the text only, not Table 4.

findings.claim: Moving the exhaust of heavy-duty vehicles to a vertical outlet is reported to cut near-ground concentrations by 65-87% without changing total emissions.
findings.value: 65 to 87% reduction in local concentration near ground (heavy-duty vehicles)
findings.quote: A vertical exhaust pipe in a heavy-duty vehicle reduces the concentration of exhaust pollutants near the ground (close to in-pram baby breathing level) and thus could help to limit the personal exposure to the elevated local concentrations of the emitted pollutants by 65 to 87%.
findings.locator: Section 6.1, citing Faiz et al. 1996 (World Bank)
findings.caveats: Heavy-duty vehicles only; method (model or field) not stated; 'could help to limit'. Supports the principle that tailpipe height matters near the ground, but is not evidence on scooters or electrification.
findings.useOnSite: A World Bank report cited by the review says raising heavy-vehicle exhausts to a vertical pipe cuts near-ground exposure by 65-87%.
findings.checkerNote: Verified. Chain link relabelled 7-break (source removal/raising), since it is not about electric vehicles.

findings.claim: No scientific study has quantified the effectiveness of pram covers; they are hypothesised to help at hotspots in cold weather but could trap heat in hot weather.
findings.value: No effect size
findings.quote: The scientific studies have not quantified the effectiveness of pram covers in mitigating exposure concentrations of in-pram babies.
findings.caveats: Hypotheses cited to BBC 2017 and Kumar et al. 2017; heat concern cited to Grounsell 2015 and Payton 2018 (grey literature). The review calls for studies of efficacy 'under diverse weather conditions'. Relevant to a warm climate.
findings.useOnSite: The authors state that the effect of pram covers on a baby's exposure has not been measured.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: Roadside passive barriers gave modest reductions: parked cars 15%, low boundary walls 12%, parked cars plus wall an increase of 6% (Gallagher et al. 2013, Dublin); a tree stand up to 22% reduction in BC (Brantley et al. 2014).
findings.value: Parked cars -15%; low boundary wall -12%; combined +6%; tree stand up to -22% BC
findings.quote: parked car model provided the highest overall average reductions of 15% in contrast to other passive control models e.g., LBW model (reduction of 12%); combined parked cars and LBW model (increase of 6%)
findings.caveats: Gallagher et al. 2013 is 'a combined measurement and modelling case study' (reference title): the review does not say which of these percentages were modelled. The pollutant and the quantity reduced (concentration or personal exposure) are not stated. Brantley et al. 2014: tree stand on an open highway, BC. Neither is specific to prams. One combination increased exposure.
findings.useOnSite: Roadside barriers cut exposure by roughly 12-22% in studies cited by the review, and one combination made it worse.
findings.checkerNote: Verified. Added that measured versus modelled is not stated for Gallagher and the reduced quantity is not specified.

findings.claim: Nanofibre and other filters reach 95-99.99+% removal of fine particles in laboratory conditions (Table 6); photocatalytic surfaces are proposed for NOx. No filtration or photocatalytic device is shown in the review to reduce a baby's exposure in a pram.
findings.value: Table 6: silk fibroin membrane 98.8% (PM2.5) and 96.2% (PM0.3); electrospun filters 99.97-99.9999%; commercial dust masks 25-97%; photocatalyst efficiency depends on TiO2 amount and sunlight (no figure)
findings.quote: Commercially available dust masks ... 25-97; The innovative passive control technology options such as nanofiber filtration technology for PM and PCO for NOx could potentially reduce exposure of in-pram babies
findings.caveats: Laboratory filter efficiencies. Filters are described as bulky, non-transparent and hindering airflow; gas-phase filtration transfers pollutants between phases. Authors name a commercial device ('BRIZI baby') and acknowledge Brizi Ltd.
findings.useOnSite: The review treats pram filtration as a promising idea; it reports laboratory filter efficiencies, not measured benefit to babies.
findings.checkerNote: Reader's '95-99.99+%' excluded the 25-97% dust-mask row; claim and value now separate the rows. Checked the Table 6 image: 98.8%/96.2% and 25-97% confirmed.

findings.claim: The review recommends low-congestion routes and keeping a safe distance from roadside polluting sources, but gives no measured evidence of the benefit of route choice; electric vehicles are not discussed.
findings.value: n/a; Liao et al. 2015 Nanchang survey of 989 parents: 69% thought air worse than 3 years ago, 97% wanted more government funding; Ginja et al. 2017: 19% of very short (~1.6 km) trips to school by car in Great Britain
findings.quote: choosing low congestion routes for transporting in-pram babies and ensuring that they maintain safe distances from the polluting mobile sources on roadsides
findings.caveats: Policy instruments named: congestion charging scheme and low emission zone (Section 8). Their measured effects are in SI S5.2, not seen. The review also says community talk in a Nairobi study included 'removing old vehicles' (Ngo et al. 2017), without data. No mention of electrification, zero-emission vehicles or scooters.
findings.useOnSite: The authors recommend low-congestion routes and distance from traffic but offer no measurements of how much this helps.
findings.checkerNote: Verified. Ginja figure is ambiguously worded in the review (very short and short trips combined).

findings.claim: UNICEF (2017) is cited that almost 17 million children under 1 year live where PM2.5 exceeds the WHO guideline by at least six times, about 12 million of them in South Asia.
findings.value: ~17 million infants; >=6x WHO PM2.5 value; ~12 million in South Asia
findings.quote: almost 17 million children < 1 year old live in highly affected regions of the world where air pollution levels exceed World Health Organization recommended values of PM2.5 by at least six times. Of which, approximately 12 million affected babies are from South Asia (UNICEF, 2017).
findings.caveats: Ambient PM2.5, not street-level or traffic-specific; South Asia, not Taiwan. No East Asian or Taiwan data. Poorer children are said to be most vulnerable (Mehta et al. 2014, Ho Chi Minh City; Perera 2017).
findings.useOnSite: UNICEF figures cited by the review say about 12 million infants in South Asia live in air at least six times the WHO PM2.5 guideline.
findings.checkerNote: Verified.

findings.claim: The review says fresh exhaust particles consist of a non-volatile core that grows by condensation of semi-volatile material, 'primarily hydrocarbons', during dilution and cooling, so nucleation and fresh emissions matter for prams very close to the road.
findings.value: n/a (qualitative)
findings.quote: The exhaust from vehicles also includes a non-volatile core and such particles grow by condensation of semi-volatile material, primarily hydrocarbons, during dilution and cooling (Kumar et al., 2011).
findings.caveats: Qualitative, one sentence, not specific to gasoline or two-wheelers; no hydrocarbon or benzene concentrations. Cited to Kumar et al. 2011 (review).
findings.useOnSite: The review notes that exhaust particles grow by condensation of hydrocarbons as the exhaust dilutes and cools.
findings.checkerNote: Missed by reader; the only place the main text links exhaust hydrocarbons to particles. Does not mention benzene or CO concentrations.

findings.claim: Street exposure is only part of a child's dose: in Barcelona, personal BC was 20% higher than at fixed school stations, and indoor environments (classroom and home) contributed 56% of the BC dose (Rivas et al. 2016); transport made a significant contribution to daily UFP dose despite a negligible share of time (Buonanno et al. 2013).
findings.value: Personal BC 20% higher than fixed stations; indoor 56% of BC dose
findings.quote: Indoor environments (classroom and home) contributed to 56% BC dose.
findings.caveats: Schoolchildren, not babies in prams; BC, not benzene or particles by number. The review's scope excludes indoor environments. The Buonanno row says transportation and cooking activities made a 'significant contribution' to the daily dose; no figure is printed.
findings.useOnSite: Cited studies show indoor settings contributed more than half of schoolchildren's black carbon dose in one Barcelona study, so time on the street is a part, not the whole, of a child's exposure.
findings.checkerNote: Missed as a finding (reader listed it only under complications). Quote verified in Table 1 on PDF page 3.

findings.claim: In Malmo, Sweden, neighbourhood socioeconomic status predicted children's NO2 exposure: exposure at home and school increased as neighbourhood socioeconomic status decreased (Chaix et al. 2006; modelled).
findings.value: n/a (no numbers)
findings.quote: Exposure to NO2 at the place of residence and school regularly increased as the socioeconomic status of a child's neighbourhood decreased.
findings.caveats: NO2 obtained through modelling (AERMOD, multilevel models), not measured; 29,133 children aged 7-15; Table 1 notes 'data obtained through modelling'. Not traffic-source-specific in the review.
findings.useOnSite: A Swedish study cited by the review found children in lower-status neighbourhoods had higher modelled NO2 exposure at home and school.
findings.checkerNote: Missed by reader. Relevant to who gets the highest dose; modelled, Sweden.

findings.claim: The review cites DEFRA (2018) that long-term PM exposure is quantified at about 340,000 life years lost in the UK, and that short-term NO2 exposure is linked with airway inflammation and greater vulnerability to respiratory infections and allergens.
findings.value: 340,000 life years lost (UK, long-term PM)
findings.quote: the long-term health impacts of PM concentrations is quantified in the range of 340,000 life years lost in the UK
findings.caveats: UK, all-source PM, not traffic or children specific; period and method not given in the review. Source: DEFRA 2018 (Clean air strategy 2018).
findings.useOnSite: The review cites the UK government for about 340,000 life years lost to long-term PM exposure (UK, all sources).
findings.checkerNote: Missed by reader; population-level figure, not specific to scooters or babies.

limitations: Authors: 'there are numerous studies on the exposure assessment of young children but similar studies for in-pram babies are very limited' (p.263) and 'only a handful have focused on in-pram babies' (p.275).

Authors: need 'diverse datasets for in-pram babies' exposure' and 'more experimental studies ... to build an exposure profiling database in diverse roadside and traffic environments'; better understanding of dispersion and flow around prams (p.275).

Authors: no study has quantified pram cover effectiveness; 'studies are needed to provide scientific evidences on the efficacy of pram covers for various pollutants and under diverse weather conditions' (p.265).
Authors: further research needed on the impact of community empowerment and public policy instruments (p.275).
Authors: Galea et al. 2014 found no consistent difference and 'did not explain the reason for this changing trend' (p.266).
Authors exclude indoor environments from scope (p.264); supplementary material not available in the PDF checked.

Checker: only four studies are compared with adults in Table 3, all from the UK, Spain or the USA, with different instruments, heights, averaging times and pollutants (PM2.5, UFP, NO2); no significance tests or CIs are reproduced for child/adult differences (only 'significantly' for Kumar morning), and Table 3 mixes means with ranges.
Checker: no systematic search strategy or study-quality appraisal; 'up to ~60%' rests on a single US study whose methods get one line in the review.

Checker: no study in the review reports benzene, CO or hydrocarbon concentrations at pram height (CO measured by Buzzard but not reported), none distinguishes gasoline from diesel, and none covers two-wheelers or idling queues at a red light.
Checker: the health-effect section concerns school-age children and adults; the claim of frontal lobe and brain-development damage to in-pram babies is an extrapolation (p.268).

Checker: the review's abstract and conclusions attribute the 0.55-0.85 m breathing-height range to the pram classification, but Table 2 gives only handle heights; the range matches the sensor heights of the Table 3 studies.
Checker: authors have an industrial collaborator (Brizi Ltd.) that makes a pram clean-air product the review discusses, and no conflict-of-interest statement is printed.
complications: Kumar et al. 2017 (Guildford): in the morning, in-pram babies had 5% significantly LOWER PM2.5 than adults (Table 3); the baby excess was 10% only in the afternoon; heights and CIs not given.
Galea et al. 2014 (Edinburgh): children in buggies not exposed to higher PM2.5 than adults; adults 17-51% higher on some days; children higher on only 1 of 6 days (16%).

The headline 'up to ~60%' is one study (Buzzard 2009, PM2.5 199 vs 125 ug/m3); the other three quantified studies show roughly 5-15% (NO2 5-15%; UFP 10%; afternoon PM2.5 10%), without confidence intervals.

The review says that within the first two metres the decreasing concentration profile with height 'does not really exist' because of traffic turbulence (p.268), weakening a simple 'lower is worse' claim and the authors' own causal explanation for the baby-height excess (p.274).

Metals in roadside particles are attributed by the review's sources mainly to tyre, brake and road dust, not exhaust (Harrison 2003; Thorpe & Harrison 2008), so the 'toxic metals' brain-damage claim does not point to tailpipes or support electrification alone; electric vehicles also produce brake, tyre and resuspended dust.

Iskandar et al.: weak non-significant association between UFPs and children's asthma admissions, significant for NOx, NO2, PM2.5, PM10. Khreis NOx CI 0.89-2.45 includes 1 although the review calls the associations significant.
Pram-cover hypothesis may backfire in heat (traps heat, restricts air circulation); no evidence of effect; relevant in a warm climate.
Barriers: the combined parked cars plus low wall model increased exposure by 6% (Gallagher 2013); effects of single barriers 12-22% only.
Rivas 2016 / Buonanno 2013: indoor settings contributed 56% of schoolchildren's BC dose in one Barcelona study; street exposure is part of total dose.

Internal tension on Kumar 2017: Table 1 attributes higher morning fine particles to higher morning traffic emissions; p.269 says traffic volume was similar in morning and afternoon. The Introduction sentence on afternoon versus morning PM2.5 is ambiguous.

The review concerns prams pushed by an adult and does not address riders, roadside workers or older people; it never mentions scooters, motorcycles, idling queues, electric vehicles, benzene or Taiwan; its source discussion is about diesel vehicles; all pram studies are from the UK, Spain or the USA.
correctionsToAbstractLevelNotes: The abstract's 'up to ~60% higher average concentrations' is the extreme end from one US study (Buzzard 2009, 59%); other studies show about 5-15% and one (Kumar 2017 morning) shows babies 5% lower. 'Up to' is accurate but is not typical.

The abstract's breathing-height range of 0.55-0.85 m is stated by the authors to come from the pram classification, but Table 2 lists only handle heights (59-124 cm); the numbers match the sensor heights in the cited Table 3 studies (0.55, 0.8, 0.85 m). Not a measurement of babies in prams by the authors.

The abstract says toxic metals 'have been shown to damage their frontal lobe as well as cognition and brain development when inhaled by in-pram babies'. The full text shows this is extrapolated from school-children studies (Barcelona, Boston) and Mexico City residents; no in-pram baby brain outcome was measured, and the review's sources say most trace metals come from wear products rather than exhaust.
The abstract implies a wide evidence base; only four studies are quantified against adults and one (Galea) found no consistent difference.
The abstract says nothing about vehicle type; the emission and mitigation discussion is diesel/heavy-duty centred, with no gasoline, scooter, motorcycle or electric content.

The Introduction (p.263) sentence on Kumar 2017 (afternoon pick-up higher than morning drop-off) is ambiguous against Table 1; Table 1 and Table 3 say morning PM2.5, PM1 and PNC were 47, 31, 31% higher than afternoon, and babies were 10% above adults only in the afternoon.
Abstract 'active and passive mitigation' sounds evidence-based; the full text states pram-cover effect is unquantified and filtration data are laboratory efficiencies.
Reader note correction: Table 1 has Barcelona x3 entries (Rivas 2016, Garcia-Algar 2015, Rivas 2014), not x4; conclusions bullet 2 is on p.274, not p.275.

answersToQuestions: 1. Narrative review (no systematic protocol printed) of scientific and grey literature on in-pram babies' outdoor exposure to traffic pollution (PM10, PM2.5, UFP, BC, NOx/NO2; p.262-263). Table 1 lists 10 studies: UK (Guildford; Edinburgh x2), Spain (Barcelona x3), Italy (Casino), Switzerland (Zurich), USA (Morgantown WV), Sweden (Malmo). Four are compared with adults in Table 3 plus Galea 2014 in text. It also classifies prams from catalogues (Table 2) and reviews dispersion, particle chemistry, mitigation and community/policy measures. No total count of papers reviewed is printed. Benzene, CO and hydrocarbon concentrations are not reported.

2. 'breathing height between 0.55 m and 0.85 m above the ground level' (abstract; p.266; p.274). Table studies: 0.55 m infant in stroller vs 1.70 m adult (Garcia-Algar); 0.8 m child vs 2.0 m adult (Kenagy); 0.85 m baby in stroller vs 1.65 m adult (Buzzard). Pram handle heights 59-124 cm, widths 56-82 cm (Table 2, p.265-266); abstract 'up to ~1.25 m'. Tailpipes: 'the first 1 m above the road level, the same height where tailpipe of most road vehicles resides' (p.265); no tailpipe height in metres and no toddler-specific breathing height. The authors say the range came from the pram classification, but Table 2 gives only handle heights. Vertical profiles measured at 0.20, 1.0 and 2.60 m (Kumar 2008b, p.268).

3. Cited measured differences (Table 3, p.267): Buzzard 2009, Morgantown USA, PM2.5 199 vs 125 ug/m3, 59% higher at 0.85 vs 1.65 m. Kenagy 2016, Edinburgh kerbside tubes, NO2 57 vs 52 ug/m3, 5-15% higher at 0.8 vs 2.0 m. Garcia-Algar 2015, Barcelona, UFP 4.82 vs 4.31 x 10^4 per cm3, 10% higher at 0.55 vs 1.70 m. Kumar, Rivas & Sachdeva 2017, Guildford, PM2.5 afternoon 9-20 vs 8-17 ug/m3, babies 10% higher; morning 10-36 vs 10-46, babies 5% significantly lower. No difference or reverse: Galea 2014, Edinburgh, PM2.5, adults 17-51% higher on some days, no difference on others, children 16% higher on 1 of 6 days; and Kumar 2017 morning. Review: 'majority of studies show increased exposure' and 'up to ~59% higher' (p.266). No CIs printed.

4. Reasons (p.263): children 'inhale a higher dose of airborne particles relative to their lung size and body weight'; 'the respiratory rate of child per body weight is generally two-fold higher than that for adults (Ginsberg et al., 2005)'; immature tissues, lungs, immune system and brain 'which continue developing quickly'; permeable respiratory membrane lining (Bates 1995; Buonanno 2013; Burtscher & Schuepp 2012; Mendell & Heath 2005; WHO 2005). Deng et al. 2018 CFD modelling: infants at greater risk, deposition decreases with age. Burtscher & Schuepp 2012: 50,000 particles/cm3 near a busy road gives about 2.5 x 10^8 particles/min for a child (calculation from a peak value). Poorer children more vulnerable (Mehta 2014; Perera 2017). Only the two-fold rate has a number; no L/min or age-specific data.

5. Hotspots: Kumar 2017 (Guildford): 'Traffic intersections found to be hotspots of enhanced exposure for PM2.5-10 and PNC'; a bus stand was assessed (no result given); morning drop-in vs afternoon pick-up: PM2.5, PM1, PNC 47, 31, 31% higher in the morning, coarse 70% higher in the afternoon (Table 1, p.264). Pram covers hypothesised at 'traffic intersections and bus stands' (p.265, untested). Rivas 2014: outdoor PM2.5 at Barcelona schools almost double usual background. No numbers for intersections or bus stops, nothing on waiting at crossings, idling or red-light queues. Introduction sentence on Kumar 2017 is ambiguous against Table 1.

6. Nothing on two-wheelers: scooter, motorcycle, moped, electric vehicle and Taiwan do not appear. Source discussion is diesel and heavy-duty (p.270). Asia: UNICEF 2017 about 12 million of almost 17 million infants in highly polluted regions are in South Asia (p.262); Chinese perception surveys such as Liao 2015, Nanchang, 989 parents (p.273); Kumar et al. 2018a on Asian transport microenvironments cited only for missing UFP/BC regulations; Mehta 2014 (Ho Chi Minh City) in the reference list for poverty and exposure. No Asian pram-height measurements.

7. Mitigation: pram covers unquantified, may trap heat (p.265). Route choice and distance from traffic recommended (p.274), no effect measured. Barriers (p.273): parked cars 15%, low boundary wall 12%, both combined +6% (Gallagher 2013, Dublin; measurement and modelling), vegetation up to 22% BC (Brantley 2014). Vertical exhaust on heavy-duty vehicles 65-87% lower local concentration (Faiz 1996, p.270). Source after-treatment (Table 4, diesel-oriented): wall-flow DPF 90% PM, SCR 75-90% / 83-88% NOx; text: CO and hydrocarbons >95%, NOx >80% with controls (p.270). Filters (Table 6, p.272): silk fibroin 98.8% PM2.5, dust masks 25-97%; photocatalytic NOx removal proposed; none tested on babies in prams. Pram height as a mitigation is not discussed beyond classification.

8. Gaps (p.275): 'only a handful have focused on in-pram babies'; need 'diverse datasets', an 'exposure profiling database in diverse roadside and traffic environments', better flow/dispersion understanding, research on community and policy effects; no pram-cover evidence; no explanation for Galea's variability. Most quotable calibrated conclusion: 'in-pram babies or children breathing height between 0.55 m and 0.85 m above the ground level with up to ~59% higher exposure than adults, depending on factors such as: (i) concentration decay with height, (ii) proximity with the roadways, (iii) location of the vehicle tailpipe close to the passenger side, and (iv) duration of exposure measurement' (p.266), paired with: most quantified studies found about 5-15%, one found babies lower in the morning, and 'There is clearly a need for further studies' (p.275).
